title: How do you answer "Tell me about yourself" in a consulting interview?
description: A structure for "Tell me about yourself" in consulting interviews, a weak and a strong example answer, and what makes the difference.
hook: It is usually the first question, and it sets the tone for everything after. Many candidates either recite their CV or ramble. A strong answer is a 60 to 90 second story with a clear thread.
body:
The question

Tell me about yourself.

A weak answer

I studied economics at Manchester, then I joined a bank as an analyst, where I did a lot of financial modelling. I also did some volunteering and I like football. Now I'm looking to move into consulting because I like problem solving.

Why it falls short: It is a list of facts with no thread, no proof of impact and a generic reason for consulting.

A strong answer

I've always been drawn to messy problems with numbers behind them. At university I ran the investment society and grew it from 40 to 200 members by changing how we ran events. At the bank I built a model that helped my team cut loan approval time by two days, and the part I enjoyed most was presenting it to senior people and getting them to act. That's why I'm excited about consulting: doing that kind of work across different industries, faster, and with clients.

Why it works: It has a thread (messy problems with numbers), two quick proof points with results, and a "why now" that leads naturally into the next question.

Make it your own

Copy the shape of the strong answer, not its words. Write your own version of "Tell me about yourself" in five or six sentences from a real moment, then say it aloud until it sounds natural.

Make the transitions in your story do the work

A strong introduction is not a chronological tour of every job. It is a short explanation of what you have chosen to do, what you learnt and why this role follows naturally. For an answer around 60–90 seconds, select two relevant experiences and end with a specific reason consulting fits your next step. The interviewer can ask for detail later.

Here is an illustrative answer for someone moving from analytics to consulting: "I studied engineering because I enjoyed solving unfamiliar problems with data. In my first role, I analysed order delays for a retailer and found that a small number of suppliers caused most of the late deliveries. I enjoyed the analysis, but even more, I liked working with procurement and operations to put the findings into practice. I later led a student volunteering project, where I learnt to persuade people without formal authority. Both experiences made me want a career combining analytical work with decisions that affect how organisations operate. That is why I am applying to consulting." Use the shape, not the wording.

Notice the links between decisions: engineering led to analysis, analysis exposed the business problem, and delivery work prompted an interest in consulting. There is no need to claim you have always dreamt of joining a firm.

Test your own answer: after hearing it once, can a friend say what you are good at and why you are changing roles? Remove details that do not help them answer those two questions. Do not invent achievements to make the narrative more dramatic.
